stories.title: Blackstone Reports 3Q 2026 Profit Dip Amid Interest Rate Headwinds
stories.excerpt: Blackstone’s third quarter earnings beat expectations but the private equity giant still experienced a more than 9 percent profit drop, which it blamed in part on its commercial real estate business confronting higher capital costs. Distributable earnings at Blackstone fell 9.2 percent year-over-year to $1.72 billion, or $1.32 a share. The firm beat analyst expectations of $1.26 per share. “The third quarter of 2026 represented a highly complex environment characterized by an historic increase in bond yields globally, including U.S. Treasury yields hitting the highest level in decades,” Stephen Schwarzman, chairman and CEO of Blackstone, said in its earnings call Thursday morning. “A higher cost of capital has negatively impacted investor settlement and transaction activity and triggered significant volatility in the markets.” The company’s distributable earnings with its real estate segment fell 10 percent to $1.68 billion. Its core-plus real estate funds reported positive appreciation of 1.6 percent in the quarter with opportunistic funds declining 3.2 percent. The firm’s flagship private real estate investment trust (BREIT), also raised $1.3 billion in the third quarter. Jon Gray, president and chief operating officer at Blackstone, said valuation cap rates increased across its holdings in the third quarter in response interest rate volatility. That led to depreciation in its opportunistic real estate funds. Gray said. He stressed, though, that Blackstone is still well positioned with its CRE business. That’s because of sharp demand within its data center and logistics holdings, which represent 54 percent of its global real estate holdings, coupled with shrinking supply in other property sectors. “This doesn’t mean there won’t be legacy equity and debt investments in real estate that will face renewed pressure from higher rates, particularly in lower growth sectors,” Gray said. “But, in this cycle as with past cycles, we believe we are in a differenti
bullets: Blackstone 3Q26 distributable earnings fell 9.2% YoY to $1.72B amid higher bond yields globally.
Real estate segment earnings down 10% to $1.68B; core-plus funds appreciated 1.6%, opportunistic declined 3%.
CEO Schwarzman cited historic Treasury yield increases and volatility dampening investor activity and transaction volume.
stories.summary: Blackstone reported Q3 2026 earnings of $1.32/share (beating guidance of $1.26) but a 9.2% year-over-year profit decline, with the real estate segment down 10% to $1.68B. The firm blamed a sharp rise in global bond yields and U.S. Treasuries hitting decade highs, which raised cost of capital and triggered market volatility. This signals a stress environment for RE investors, particularly in opportunistic strategies that declined 3% in the quarter.
stories.impact: Rising rates and bond yields directly pressure development underwriting across all markets: cap rates must rise to compete with fixed income, refinancing costs spike, and leverage-dependent acquisitions become uneconomical. Blackstone's scale and reach mean a pullback here signals tighter capital availability broadly, lengthening the window for developers already in-contract or with construction financing locked in. Markets most exposed to speculative development (luxury, office conversion) face the sharpest headwinds.

stories.title: CB Equities Offloads 64K-SF Charlotte Flex Office Building
stories.excerpt: CB Equities offloaded Forest Park IV at 600 Forest Point Circle for $11 million. CB paid $9.2 million for the 64,000-square-foot Charlotte office building in 2023. Greenleaf Capital Partners was the buyer. The Charlotte Business Chronicle reports that CB converted it into a flex office property. It has 16-foot clear heights, three dock-high doors, a drive-in door and parking for 360 vehicles. Built in 1999, the property is part of the Forest Park business park. Forest Park IV is 100% leased to Flexential, Tranzact and Preferred Electric Co. CBRE’s Matt Smith, Patrick Gildea, Robert Hardaway, Kris Westmoreland and Alek Salfia represented the seller in the transaction. On its website, CB says it has identified and remains hyper-focused on three primary investment markets poised for population and economic growth in the short, medium and long terms. They have established presences in each of these three markets: the Greater Boston Metro Area, the Charlotte Metropolitan Area, and Southeast Florida. The post CB Equities Offloads 64K-SF Charlotte Flex Office Building appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: CB Equities sold Charlotte flex office (64K SF) to Greenleaf Capital for $11M, up from $9.2M purchase in 2023.
Building 100% leased to Flexential, Tranzact, Preferred Electric; features 16-ft clear heights, dock doors, 360 parking.
CB Equities hyper-focused on Greater Boston, Charlotte metro, Southeast Florida for identified growth.
stories.summary: CB Equities exited a Charlotte flex office asset (Forest Park IV, 600 Forest Point Circle) to Greenleaf Capital Partners for $11 million, realizing a $1.8M gain on a 2023 acquisition of $9.2M. The 64,000-SF 1999-built property features light-industrial specs (16-ft ceilings, dock doors, ample parking) and is 100% leased to three tenants. CB's stated investment thesis focuses on Greater Boston, Charlotte metro, and Southeast Florida.
stories.impact: The Charlotte sale signals that flex/light-industrial assets remain attractive to acquisition capital in growth metros, but CB's $1.9M profit over three years (~20% IRR) may not fully justify hold if cap rates on exit were compressed by rate environment. Charlotte continues to draw capital; a developer seeing this should monitor lease expirations and vacancy in adjacent flex parks—demand signal is strong, but pricing discipline matters. CB's retreat suggests they may redeploy to Boston or Miami where fundamentals are tighter.

stories.title: Historic Worcester Boys Club Incorporated into Age-Restricted Housing Development
stories.excerpt: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey and Worcester city officials cut the ribbon Wednesday on The Residences on Lincoln Square, a hybrid development that transformed the historic Worcester Boys Club building into 16 apartment homes and community spaces, while erecting an adjacent 64-unit, five-story apartment development. The $51-million project from WinnCompanies delivers 80 affordable, energy-efficient apartment homes for adults 55 and older. The community is fully leased. Sixty-eight apartments are leased to households earning up to 60% of Area Median Income (AMI) and 12 units are occupied by those earning up to 30% AMI. Eleven serve as housing for residents with disabilities. “In one of the state’s most essential housing markets, the Residences on Lincoln Square provides the senior population of the Worcester area a long-term home of outstanding quality and convenience,” said WinnCompanies CEO Gilbert Winn. “Reviving this iconic building has been a city priority for two decades. An innovative development plan and the fantastic support of our public and private partners finally made it happen.” The post Historic Worcester Boys Club Incorporated into Age-Restricted Housing Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: WinnCompanies delivered 80 affordable units (16 adaptive reuse + 64 new construction) in Worcester, MA; $51M total project cost.
68 units at 60% AMI, 12 at 30% AMI, 11 for disability housing; 100% leased at opening.
Historic Boys Club adaptive reuse core to 20-year city priority; project fully entitled and funded with public/private support.
stories.summary: WinnCompanies completed The Residences on Lincoln Square in Worcester, MA, a $51M hybrid development delivering 80 affordable senior apartments (age 55+), combining 16 units in an adaptive-reuse of the historic Worcester Boys Club with a new 64-unit five-story building. All units are income-restricted (68 at 60% AMI, 12 at 30% AMI); the project is 100% leased at opening and includes 11 units for residents with disabilities. The project resolved a two-decade city priority.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on market-rate multifamily development. However, this signals Worcester's entitlement and financing infrastructure is mature enough to support mixed-income projects with historic preservation components. For developers, it shows that 100% affordable senior housing can lease quickly when well-located and subsidized. The tight integration of adaptive reuse + new construction is a model; Worcester's workforce growth and aging population may support additional market-rate or workforce housing nearby, but this project does not add pressure to Worcester's rental market.

stories.title: Broe Group Makes First SoCal Multifamily Acquisition in San Diego
stories.excerpt: Broe Real Estate Group (BREG), the real estate affiliate of Colorado investment firm The Broe Group, has acquired 525 Olive in San Diego. Although the purchase price in the all-cash deal was not disclosed, the 20-story, 204-unit luxury apartment building adjacent to Balboa Park was valued at about $100 million when it was delivered in August 2022. Walker & Dunlop’s Hunter Combs advised on the transaction, which was completed in 60 days. “525 Olive is San Diego’s premier luxury living community in San Diego’s most desirable submarket,” said BREG SVP of investments Milan Gutesha. “San Diego’s dynamic economy, high-quality work force, and exceptional quality of life made this market a priority for our multifamily expansion. This acquisition reflects the very best of San Diego as we continue to explore further market expansion.” While The Broe Group has existing rail and real estate holdings in California, the 525 Olive acquisition marks its entry into Southern California’s multifamily market. The post Broe Group Makes First SoCal Multifamily Acquisition in San Diego appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Broe Real Estate Group acquired 525 Olive, San Diego (204 luxury units, 20-story); valued ~$100M on 2022 delivery.
All-cash purchase; transaction closed in 60 days; asset adjacent to Balboa Park in premier submarket.
First SoCal multifamily entry for Broe; firm cites San Diego's economy, workforce quality, QOL as expansion rationale.
stories.summary: Broe Real Estate Group (BREG), the real estate arm of Denver-based The Broe Group, acquired 525 Olive in San Diego, a 204-unit luxury apartment tower delivered in August 2022 and valued at approximately $100 million. The all-cash transaction closed in 60 days and marks BREG's first multifamily acquisition in Southern California, despite The Broe Group's existing rail and real estate holdings in California. BREG SVP Milan Gutesha cited San Diego's dynamic economy, quality workforce, and quality of life as drivers of the investment thesis.
stories.impact: A large, out-of-state institutional buyer entering San Diego multifamily signals confidence in the market's fundamentals and a tightening cap rate environment that rewards core-plus/stabilized assets. All-cash acquisition by BREG suggests portfolio recycling and modest yield compression vs. leverage-based buyers. San Diego's supply pipeline and absorption should be monitored: if BREG's entry catalyzes additional institutional capital flows, rent growth may accelerate, tightening the window for development acquisitions. The Balboa Park submarket's desirability and Broe's scale suggest they see long-term hold opportunity in a supply-constrained, high-barrier market.

stories.title: Northwind Doubles Target with $1B CRE Debt Fund Raise
stories.excerpt: Northwind Group, a New York-based real estate private equity and debt fund manager, has reached the final close of Northwind Debt Fund III (NDF III) with $1 billion in committed capital, doubling its $500-million target and making it the largest fund in Northwind’s history. NDF III continues Northwind’s flagship real estate credit strategy, which the firm launched in 2017. The fund primarily originates senior-secured bridge loans across major U.S. gateway markets, with a focus on acquisition, bridge, condo inventory, construction, office-to-residential conversions, pre-development, lease-up and other specialized financing solutions. “The final close of NDF III is a defining milestone for Northwind and a strong endorsement of our growing credit platform,” said Ran Eliasaf, founder and managing partner. “We believe the current environment presents one of the most attractive lending opportunities we have seen, and NDF III positions us to capitalize on it on a greater scale than ever before.” The post Northwind Doubles Target with $1B CRE Debt Fund Raise appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Northwind Group closed Debt Fund III at $1B (doubled $500M target); largest fund in firm's history.
Focus on senior-secured bridge loans across gateway markets; specialties include acquisition, office-to-residential conversion, construction, lease-up.
Fund manager cites current environment as 'most attractive lending opportunity' seen; capital deployment expected to accelerate.
stories.summary: Northwind Group, a New York-based real estate credit manager, reached final close of Northwind Debt Fund III (NDF III) with $1 billion in committed capital—double its original $500M target and the firm's largest fund to date. NDF III originates senior-secured bridge loans across major U.S. gateways, with emphasis on acquisition, bridge, condo inventory, construction, office-to-residential conversions, pre-development, and lease-up financing. Founder Ran Eliasaf stated the current environment represents an unusually attractive lending opportunity and positioned the fund to capitalize on it.
stories.impact: A $1B close on a specialty construction/bridge debt fund signals strong institutional appetite for real estate credit despite rate volatility. For developers, this is critical: bridge financing and construction capital are flowing into a market where traditional bank debt is retrenching. Northwind's focus on office-to-residential conversions is a direct bet on the conversion thesis in high-cost gateways (NYC, SF, Boston, DC); developers with entitled conversion projects or in-transition office assets should expect competitive debt terms and faster underwriting. Capital availability supports development feasibility in gateway markets, though spreads and rates will reflect higher SOFR.

stories.title: Self-Storage Development Boom Shifts to Mid-Sized Urban Markets
stories.excerpt: Although self-storage development over the past decade has occurred mainly in the suburbs of large, fast-growing metro areas, the balance is shifting toward urban settings in mid-sized metro areas, Yardi’s StorageCafe reported. Among the 100 largest metro areas, 42 have seen 50% or more of their self-storage development over the past 10 years inside city limits. The firm cited Las Vegas, San Antonio and Cape Coral-Fort Myers, FL among the leading metros for urban self-storage construction. In Sun Belt cities, “rapid in-migration has delivered the renter-heavy, apartment-dense urban population that makes urban self-storage not just viable, but essential,” according to StorageCafe. “Storage is a proximity business,” said Victor Maghear, consumer trends and market analyst at StorageCafe. “Customers want convenient access, and that makes urban sites attractive even when development costs are higher. What’s interesting is how differently that opportunity plays out across markets — some are still expanding outward, while others are putting more of their next projects inside city boundaries.” The post Self-Storage Development Boom Shifts to Mid-Sized Urban Markets appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Self-storage development shifting from suburbs to urban centers in mid-sized metros; 42 of 100 largest metros show 50%+ urban development.
Las Vegas, San Antonio, Cape Coral-Fort Myers leading urban self-storage construction; Sun Belt in-migration driving renter-dense, apartment-heavy populations.
Urban self-storage viable due to proximity demand and rental populations; development costs higher but customer convenience justifies location.
stories.summary: Self-storage development over the past decade shifted from suburban sprawl toward urban infill in mid-sized metro areas, according to StorageCafe analysis. Among the 100 largest U.S. metros, 42 have seen 50% or more of self-storage development in city limits over the past 10 years. Las Vegas, San Antonio, and Cape Coral-Fort Myers are leading urban markets; StorageCafe attributes this to rapid in-migration in Sun Belt cities creating renter-heavy, apartment-dense urban populations where proximity and convenience offset higher development costs.
stories.impact: Indirect signal for multifamily developers: urban self-storage expansion correlates with and follows renter population density and migration inflows. In Las Vegas, San Antonio, and Florida metros, this suggests apartment demand (and thus multifamily fundamentals) remain strong enough to support complementary storage demand at urban locations. The shift toward urban storage is a lagging indicator of successful multifamily in-migration; developers should track self-storage permitting and starts as a proxy for apartment demand confirmation in secondary/tertiary Sun Belt markets.

stories.title: Real Estate Tech Startup MARC Raises $5M Seed Round
stories.excerpt: MARC, an AI platform that helps institutional real estate owners identify and streamline operating costs across their portfolios, announced Thursday that it raised $5 million in an oversubscribed Seed round. Work-Bench led the round with MXV Capital participating. The latest raise brings MARC’s total funding to $6 million, with participation from founders and operators including Des Traynor (Intercom), Mark Ghermezian (Braze), Ian Nolan (Brightflag), Cyrus Claffey (ButterflyMX), Daniel Eberhard (Koho) and Brian Moran, the manager of professional golfer Shane Lowry. Founded in January 2026, the Manhattan-based startup plans to use the funding to accelerate its expansion across the U.S. and Canada, said Aaron Devitt, the 24-year-old founder and CEO of MARC. A self-described college dropout in Ireland, Devitt previously built MARC’s first property management product there and in the U.K., recording more than 40,000 monthly logins before expanding the company into North America. “We were profitable at the start of this year and ended up getting pulled into a process from a couple of different funds on the West Coast and East Coast, so we said we might go out and try to raise 2 or 3 million, and we raised 5 million pretty quickly,” said Devitt. The startup also plans to use the new funding to grow its team in New York, he said. “We’re hiring a head of engineering at the moment in New York and we’re hiring some strategic account executives, also in New York,” Devitt said. “So we have a great problem right now that we have a lot of demand and we’re just trying to get the product out the door. But, as we continue to improve and enhance the product, we want to make sure that we have the right people on the bus, so to speak, to help us keep building the best possible product we can put into the market.” While institutional real estate owners manage billions of dollars of assets, nearly 100 percent of invoices are unverified against their underlying contracts
bullets: MARC AI platform raised $5M seed (oversubscribed) led by Work-Bench; brings total funding to $6M since January 2026 launch.
Founder Aaron Devitt (age 24) built prior PM product in Ireland/UK with 40K+ monthly logins; MARC is profitable.
Platform identifies and streamlines operating costs across institutional real estate portfolios; expanding into U.S. and Canada.
stories.summary: MARC, a Manhattan-based AI platform helping institutional real estate owners identify and reduce operating costs across portfolios, raised $5 million in an oversubscribed seed round led by Work-Bench. Total funding reached $6M with participation from entrepreneurs including Des Traynor (Intercom), Mark Ghermezian (Braze), and others. Founder Aaron Devitt, 24, previously scaled a property management product in Ireland and the U.K. to 40K+ monthly logins; MARC claims profitability and plans U.S./Canada expansion.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on development feasibility or market fundamentals. However, early-stage venture backing for operational tech (vs. development-focused tools) reflects investor thesis that institutional multifamily operators are focused on cost efficiency and portfolio optimization in a higher-rate environment. If MARC succeeds in reducing operating expense ratios, it could increase cap rates and valuations for stabilized assets, potentially tightening the development spread and making ground-up projects less competitive. Keep on radar as a signal of sector-wide cost pressure.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Joshua Young of Brown Harris Stevens
stories.excerpt: Having joined Brown Harris Stevens (BHS) in November 2021 as an executive vice president, Joshua Young went on to found his own team at BHS in June 2025. He leads the firm’s Young New Development Group, which focuses on marketing, leasing and sales of new development projects. The former Division I baseball player for St. John’s University began his career in 2006 as a project manager for Cantor Pecorella, a luxury residential development advisory and sales firm. Over the last 20 years, Young has established himself as a leader in residential sales, leasing, commercial leasing, property management and asset management, having represented properties in New York and Miami Beach. “Josh has forged an impressive career over the many years I’ve known him, and I was hoping to bring him to BHS when the moment was right,” BHS CEO Bess Freedman said in a 2021 statement about his hiring. “He has experience in every facet of commercial and residential real estate.” Commercial Observer spoke with Young in September for a series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we learn more about residential brokers and what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What has been the biggest deal of your career so far? Joshua Young: I worked on some of the most incredible spec homes built on North Bay Road in Miami Beach while with To Better Days Building. They were sold for record numbers at the time, and it was quite a learning experience. Building such large-scale homes on the waterfront brought many challenges. We worked very hard to overcome it while trying to keep the focus on Miami Beach. What is your career Everest? My career Everest hasn’t been centered around a specific building or sales number. It’s more about continuing to earn a seat at the table with the biggest and brightest developers. Young's track record in New York and Miami suggests BHS expects continued multifamily development activity in gateway markets; his hire/group launch indicates confidence in deal flow despite rate headwinds.

stories.title: Manhattan Investment Sales Dip but Remain Ahead of 2025: Report
stories.excerpt: Investment sales volume in Manhattan fell 27 percent over the third quarter of 2026, totaling $2.5 billion, yet the second straight quarterly decline coincided with continued, if slowing, annual momentum. “We’ll have our record year this year, even through all of this,” Brandon Polakoff, a principal and head of New York City investment sales at Avison Young, told Commercial Observer, referring to the decade-high of 824 citywide transactions projected for 2026. “There are good opportunities, and there is capital out there for the right opportunities,” he added. The full-year pace of sales volume remained above 2025 measures, according to Avison Young’s most recent investment sales report, but below its 10-year average, as smaller dollar amounts weight on the annual total. Deal count, however, saw a 22 percent annual uptick over the first three quarters of the year, reaching 273 sales. In the third quarter alone, Manhattan recorded 87 sales, down modestly from the previous quarter, while year-to-date dollar volume edged up 4 percent over 2025 to $9.61 billion. Manhattan’s underlying strength has kept deals moving, Polakoff said, and the gains are even stronger citywide. Across New York City, sales volume rose 13 percent across the first three quarters of 2026, reaching $16.2 billion. Market headwinds have persisted through the year. Higher interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty and rising Treasury yields remain a source of hesitation for investors. Manhattan’s buyer pool has also shifted. Private buyers have the lead, and real estate investment trusts’ (REITs) share of dollar volume grew from 7.3 percent in 2025 to 36 percent so far this year, according to Avison Young. International and foreign buyers, on the other hand, continued to pull back. Beyond the quarterly fluctuations, however, Manhattan is on track to rack up more than 360 transactions this year. bullets: Manhattan investment sales fell 27% in 3Q26 to $2.5B; second consecutive quarterly decline but year-to-date pace remains ahead of 2025.
2026 projected to close with 824 citywide transactions (decade high); deal count up 22% YoY to 273 sales in 3Q.

stories.summary: Manhattan investment sales volume declined 27% quarter-over-quarter in Q3 2026 to $2.5 billion, marking the second consecutive quarterly drop. However, year-to-date metrics remain ahead of 2025 figures, with 2026 projected to record 824 citywide transactions (the highest in a decade). While deal count rose 22% annually to 273 sales, smaller average transaction sizes are suppressing total dollar volume. Per Avison Young's Brandon Polakoff, capital remains available for selective opportunities.
stories.impact: Manhattan's market-by-market divergence matters: while volume dips, deal count and transaction velocity remain healthy, signaling selective capital deployment and price discipline rather than market collapse. For developers, this means: (1) smaller deals and mid-market asset classes (workforce, conversion) are trading, while mega-deals slow; (2) financing remains selective and rate-sensitive; (3) the 824-transaction pace suggests underlying health in market-rate residential but skews toward existing inventory vs. new development. Entry points for development financing and land acquisition may narrow, but the deal flow confirms continued demand for well-positioned assets.

stories.title: Four Signals From the New York City Market That Matter More Than a Headline
stories.excerpt: The New York City residential real estate market is often discussed as though every buyer and seller is responding to the same conditions. From the ground level, that is not what we are seeing. Clients are making very individual decisions about timing, flexibility and opportunity. Their choices reveal a market that is more strategic than hesitant. Four patterns have become especially clear in recent transactions. They are less about broad predictions and more about how people are actually moving through the city today. Sellers are renting before they buy again. For many owners, selling no longer automatically leads to an immediate purchase. Some are choosing a rental period between homes, particularly when they have sold well, but do not want to force their next decision. Claudia Saez-Fromm. PHOTO: Courtesy Claudia Saez-Fromm At 60 Warren Street, Residence 3, a Tribeca home we relaunched through the SaezFromm Team, our clients chose to rent on the Upper East Side rather than rush into another purchase. The decision gave them time to experience a different part of the city and wait for the right next home. It was not a retreat from ownership. It was a way to preserve optionality. This approach is especially sensible for clients whose needs have changed. A rental can create breathing room after a sale, without requiring them to compromise on the location, layout or building that will shape their next chapter. Investors are still finding reasons to act. The strength of New York’s rental market continues to influence buying decisions. Investors are paying close attention to homes that combine enduring location appeal with the qualities renters value most: light, thoughtful layouts, service, and access to the neighborhood. bullets: NYC residential market shows four key behavioral patterns: sellers renting before buying, rental intermediacy between sales, strategic timing, market heterogeneity.
Clients making individual decisions about timing/flexibility rather than responding to uniform market signals; example: Tribeca seller rented Upper East Side before re-purchasing.
Market behavior signals strategic positioning, not panic; rental periods between ownership reflect willingness to defer next purchase for market clarity.
stories.summary: A qualitative analysis from a residential brokerage perspective reveals four patterns in NYC's residential market that challenge blanket forecasts. Sellers increasingly rent for interim periods between sales and new purchases rather than immediately re-buying; example cited is a Tribeca seller who rented on the Upper East Side to experience neighborhoods and time the next acquisition. Clients are making highly individual decisions around timing and flexibility, suggesting strategic positioning rather than hesitance or distress.
stories.impact: This is a behavioral/demand signal for multifamily developers: a shift toward interim rental (rather than immediate repurchase) suggests (1) extended decision cycles that favor rental supply and reduce urgency for purchase; (2) discretionary migration within the city (e.g., Tribeca to Upper East Side) that may redistribute demand geographically; (3) owner-occupants (high-income sellers) entering the rental market, increasing demand for well-appointed short-term or intermediate-term rentals. For developers, this implies sustained rental demand from high-net-worth individuals and longer occupancy timelines. The qualitative tone ('strategic, not hesitant') implies NYC multifamily fundamentals remain resilient, supporting development feasibility in prime submarkets.
